about: Lundenwic (London: the wic on the Strand to 886, then the town inside the old walls), written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/lundenwic.md and the spine. One port. A draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what the sources do not show. The dossier's section 8 lists what must not be claimed and this file keeps to it: no wic-reeve, tollman or priest of 793 is named (Wighelm is the spine's invention, the office is real); no market place, quay or jetty is known (ships lay on a beach); where the king's hall and the mint stood is not known (the sites are the game's assumption); the fires of 798 and 801 rest on a twelfth-century text; no reeve is recorded turning Franks away; Frisians here in 793 are inferred; in 793 there is no bridge, no Tower, no Westminster church, no Southwark and no Billingsgate. Woven with the other ports of the region on 7 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways, beats added in Sarre, Fordwic, Dofras, Gipeswic, Hamwic and Dommoc, the story of the reeve's riddle and the gold piece placed (the spine's hooks riddle_road and silver_road), three people made real whom other files tied to (King Aethelstan, a moneyer of Cnut's day, the port-reeve Wulfgar), and the region's cards (Data/encounters/england_south_east_793.json) hung on the sites.

ports.summary: An open trading town on the gravel bank north of the Thames, a short walk upstream of the empty Roman city, held by King Offa of the Mercians. In 793 it has no wall, no bridge and no quay: ships are run onto the hard at high water and sold from where they sit, with the king's wic-reeve as witness. A merchant comes with wine, quernstones, pots and glass from the Rhine and goes home with cloaks, combs, hides and wool, and with whatever the reeve chose to tell him.
ports.seasons: The tide is the calendar: a ship waits at the Nore for the flood and rides it up, and the springs after each new and full moon are the days to beach and to float off. Wine comes in the dark of the year after the vintage, wool after the shearing near midsummer, stock is driven in and killed at Martinmas; no fair is recorded, the beach is the market every day but Sunday.

history.text: Saint Paul's is founded inside the old walls for Mellitus, the first bishop of the East Saxons.
Imma, a Northumbrian thegn taken in battle whom no fetter would hold, is sold at London to a Frisian, who lets him ransom himself.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History IV.22 (dossier 7 [Bd]); the year is that of the battle on the Trent

history.text: By the law of the Kentish kings a man of Kent who buys in the wic of London has two or three honest men or the king's wic-reeve as witness, and vouches his warranty at the king's hall in the wic (673-685).
history.source: Laws of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16 (Thatcher 1907, Fordham sourcebook; dossier 1 [HE])

history.text: Boniface comes to London, pays his fare to a shipmaster and sails to Dorestad.
history.source: Willibald, Life of Boniface c. 4 (dossier 4 [Wb]); not quoted, the usual translation is not free

history.text: Bede calls London the chief town of the East Saxons and a mart of many peoples coming to it by land and sea.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History II.3 (our rendering); dossier 1 [N]

history.text: King Aethelbald of the Mercians frees one ship of the bishop of Rochester from the toll at the port of London.
history.source: Sawyer S 88, confirmed by King Berhtwulf 844 x 851 (dossier 4)

history.text: King Offa confirms the freedom from toll at London of a ship of the minster in Thanet (761-764).

About this year King Charles closes his ports to English ships after a quarrel over a marriage offer; Gervold, abbot of Saint-Wandrille and keeper of the tolls from Rouen to Quentovic, helps to mend it. The dates are loose: about 789 to before 796.
history.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16; Wikipedia (en) 'Offa of Mercia', 'Gervold' (dossier 4 [Of, Ge])

history.text: King Offa's moneyers leave off the light penny for a heavier, broader one (792 or 793).

King Charles writes to King Offa of the black stones the English want and the cloaks the Franks want at the old length. Offa dies on 29 July; his son Ecgfrith reigns 141 days; Coenwulf is king by December.
history.source: Charles to Offa, 796 (in William of Malmesbury, tr. Giles 1847); chronicle_793.json (dossier 4, 5 [Of, C])

history.text: London burns with great loss of life. Pope Leo refuses to move the southern archbishopric here from Canterbury.
history.source: Historia Regum, a twelfth-century text (?); chronicle_793.json 798-london-fire-798, 798-leo-canterbury (dossier 5, 8)

history.text: Bishop Heathoberht of London dies, and soon after a great part of London burns.
King Coenwulf's council sits 'in the famous place and royal town, the wic of London'.
King Ecgberht of the West Saxons holds Mercia for a year and strikes pennies at London (829-830).
This year there was great slaughter at London, at Quentovic and at Rochester.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, printed under 839 (dossier 5, 8: the old translations' 'Canterbury' is Quentovic)

history.text: Three hundred and fifty ships come into the mouth of the Thames; the crews storm Canterbury and London and put King Beorhtwulf of the Mercians to flight.
King Burgred grants Bishop Alhhun of Worcester the plot called Ceolmundingchaga, not far from the west gate, with measure and weights 'as is the custom in the port'.
The army goes from Reading to London and takes its winter quarters there (871-872). The bishop of Worcester sells land to pay his share of the tribute, in 'the year the pagans sat in London'.
King Alfred occupies London and gives it to Ealdorman Aethelred of the Mercians. The town moves inside the old walls; the wic becomes the old wic, Ealdwic.

Bishop Waerferth of Worcester is given 'Hwaetmund's stone', an old stone building by the trading shore. Trade on the public street or the shore pays the king; the bishop keeps the urn and scales in his own court.
The men of London help to storm the Danish fort at Benfleet (893) and to take the Danish ships on the Lea (896).
Plots at Aethelred's hithe are given to Bishop Waerferth and Archbishop Plegmund, each with ship stations before the wall (898 or 899).

The bishops and reeves of London set down the rules of their peace-guild: the brothers, in tens and hundreds, pay fourpence a year, ride out together after stolen stock, and pay a man for what he lost (about 930-939).
history.source: VI Aethelstan (dossier 6, 7 [At]); not quoted, Attenborough 1922 is not free

history.text: Saint Paul's burns and is restored the same year.
London burns.
On the Nativity of Saint Mary Olaf and Swein come to London with ninety-four ships and are driven off.

About this year the toll at Billingsgate is set down: a small boat a halfpenny, a sailing ship a penny, a keel or hulk four; the Emperor's men give at Christmas and Easter two grey cloths and one brown, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two kegs of vinegar.
Thorkell's army lies in the Thames. 'Oft they fought against the city of London; but glory be to God, that it yet standeth firm.'
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1009 (Ingram 1823 (?) as the dossier gives it)

history.text: Archbishop Aelfheah, killed by the army at Greenwich on 19 April, is carried to London and buried at Saint Paul's. In 1023 King Cnut has him taken to Canterbury.
On Michaelmas eve the great sea-flood comes far up over the land and drowns many towns and people. The year before, London had submitted to Swein.
King Aethelred dies at London on Saint George's day and Edmund is chosen king there. Cnut's ships dig a ditch on the south side, drag their ships round the bridge and besiege the town.
England pays King Cnut 72,000 pounds, and London 10,500 pounds besides.
King Harthacnut dies at Lambeth on 8 June, as he stood drinking, at the wedding feast of Tovi the Proud and Gytha, Osgod Clapa's daughter.
Spearhafoc, goldsmith, abbot and bishop-elect of London, vanishes with the gold and gems given him for the king's crown.
Earl Godwin's fleet waits at Southwark for the flood and passes the bridge close by the south bank.
King Edward dies on 5 January, eight days after his church at Westminster was hallowed. Harold is king, and at Christmas William is crowned there.

eras.text: Offa's wic. Past its best: the busiest years were before 750, and some plots are rubbish dumps now, but there is a loom in almost every house and the beach is full on a spring tide. The ports of the Franks are shut to English ships, so Frankish hulls are turned away here and a Frisian is asked whose man he is. The new heavy penny is the only coin the reeve will count.

Coenwulf's royal town, and then his heirs'. The ban is over and the wine comes freely. The town burns in 798 and again in 801 (?) and is built back thinner each time. Kent rises and is harried; kings meet in council here; for one year (829-830) a West Saxon's name is on the pennies. Nothing is forbidden but what always is.

An open beach in the years of the fleets. After the slaughter of 842 and the storm of 851 ditches two metres deep are dug across the roads at the north and the back of the town. Fewer houses, more fences. The penny is worse each year, and weighing is the king's and is paid for.

The army winters here in 871-872 and the Mercians pay it to go. The king of the Mercians is driven over sea in 874. What is left of the wic trades with whoever holds the river; honest people have begun to carry their goods inside the old walls at night.

Lundenburh. King Alfred has given the town to Ealdorman Aethelred, and it lives inside the Roman walls, two kilometres east of the old beach, which is going back to fields and is called the old wic. Bishops hold plots at Aethelred's hithe with ship stations in front; trade on the street or the shore pays the king. By the 930s there are eight moneyers and a peace-guild that rides after thieves.

A rich walled town with a bridge, a toll read out at Billingsgate and the men of Rouen, Flanders and the Emperor on the bank. It burns in 982 and beats off ninety-four ships in 994. From 1009 the army is in the river most years; the town holds, pays, buries an archbishop and at last gives in to Swein.

Cnut's London. The siege, the ditch round the bridge, then 10,500 pounds and peace. Danes live in the town and lie in Saint Paul's churchyard under stones cut in their own letters; the shipmen of the fleet have a voice in choosing kings. The best years of all for a ship between Frisia, London and Denmark.

King Edward's town. A port-reeve and a staller answer for it; upriver on Thorney the king builds a great stone church in the Norman manner. Godwin's fleet passes the bridge in 1052. In the last year a king is buried and two are crowned at Westminster.

sites.name: The hard below the Strand
sites.see: A long shelving beach of gravel and cobbles on the outside of the river's bend, grey-brown at low water, with hulls sitting dry on it in a row and bigger ships riding off. Along the top runs a timber front a metre high, stakes and wattle and oak planks, with mooring posts; behind it the bank climbs to thatched roofs on the skyline. Downstream the old city wall and the church on its hill stand against the morning light. Gulls, the suck of the ebb, wet rope, river mud, wool grease.
sites.source: Killock 2019 and Cowie 1988 (Research/lundenwic_c800_notes.md; dossier 1, 2 [N]): the gravel and cobble beach, timber fronts 1 m high with mooring posts at York Buildings (oak felled 670-690), ships run onto the hard at high water. No quay or jetty (dossier 8). The pilot and the tide: Research/thames_mouth_c800_notes.md (inferred).

sites.name: The king's hall in the wic
sites.see: A long timber hall with a porch, set back from the road on the bluff with a fenced yard and a horse line. Two spearmen sit on the bench by the door. Inside it is dim and smells of rushes and smoke; the reeve stands at a table with tally sticks laid out by length, and a clerk scratches wax. Everybody who has bought anything worth swearing to is waiting his turn.
sites.source: The hall is certain from the law, its site unknown (dossier 2, 8): Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16, warranty vouched 'at the king's hall in the wic'. The porched hall is modelled on the Treasury hall at Whitehall, about 800, 5.6 m wide (dossier 2 [N]). Coenwulf's council of 811: S 168.

sites.name: The moneyers' benches
sites.see: A shed with a locked door and a smoke hole, open on one side to a counter. A man sits astride a block with a die set in it; another feeds him blanks from a bowl. Each blow is one penny, and the sound carries down the road like a slow woodpecker. On the counter a balance, a touchstone and a pan of clippings nobody is allowed to lean over.
sites.source: The mint is certain from the coin, its site unknown (dossier 2, 8 [Co]). Offa's moneyers very probably of London: Naismith 2010 (dossier 3). After 886 the moneyers work inside the walls; King Aethelstan gives London eight (II Aethelstan 14, Thatcher 1907). The bench and die are the game's picture (?).

sites.name: The road up from the shore
sites.see: A metalled road five paces wide running north from the Strand between close-set houses of wattle and daub under thatch, end-on to the street. Doors stand open; a loom thumps in nearly every one. Goods are sold from thresholds and from the tails of carts: Rhenish pots in straw, grey querns stacked like loaves, a cask with a fir-wood head, figs in a jar for somebody's lord. Pigs, woodsmoke, wet dye, hot horn.
sites.source: The 5 m metalled road with over 60 buildings at the Royal Opera House; parallel roads under James Street and Bow Street; imports of Mayen lava querns, Badorf and Tating ware, glass, Norwegian hones, figs and grapes, a silver-fir cask head (dossier 2, 4 [N]). No market place is known (dossier 8): trade is on the shore and in the street.

sites.name: Leofrun's looms
sites.see: A house wider than its neighbours with two upright looms against the back wall, rows of clay rings hanging on the warps and clicking when a shed is changed. Finished cloaks lie folded on a chest, brown and grey and one dyed with madder. A woman measures a length along her arm and a girl counts the rings aloud. Lanolin, lye and the sour smell of a dye vat in the yard.
sites.source: Loomweights in almost every house of the wic (dossier 1 [N]); cloth and cloaks as the chief export, and the cloaks 'at the old length' of the letter of 796 (dossier 4 [Of]). This house and its weaver are invented.

sites.name: The comb-maker's yard
sites.see: A small yard behind a house, white with sawdust of antler and bone. A man sits on a low bench sawing teeth into a plate clamped between his knees; finished combs hang on a string by the door and a pit in the corner is full of sawn tines and spoiled blanks. Next door a smith is drawing wire. The smell is singed horn, and it gets into the bread.
sites.source: The pit at Bedford Street with the waste of 65 to 70 combs, about 730-750; smithing at Shorts Gardens; horn and leather workers (dossier 2 [N]). The maker is invented.

sites.name: Tatberht's yard by the west road
sites.see: A fenced plot at the east end of the town, on the road that runs on to the old city's west gate. A long house with a loft, a store with a bar on the door, a well lined with an old wine cask, and a cart shed where three Frisians are arguing about freight. A dog that knows who has paid. From the gate the broken wall and the church on its hill are in plain sight over the Fleet's wide mouth.
sites.source: The plot 'Ceolmundingchaga, not far from the west gate', with measure and weights as is the custom in the port: S 208, 857 (dossier 2). Barrel-lined wells and the silver-fir cask head (dossier 2 [N]). The host answers for a guest of three nights: Hlothhere and Eadric c. 15 (npc_text_encounters.md 1.1). That this plot was a lodging for Frisians, and the family, are invented; Frisians here are inferred from Bede IV.22 and the wine casks (dossier 8).

sites.name: Wynflaed's ale-house
sites.see: A low house near the top of the beach path with a bush on a pole over the door and benches along both walls. A notched stick hangs above the lintel for every crew that owes. The fire is in the middle of the floor and the smoke finds its own way out. Four tongues at once, dice on a board, somebody asking a riddle too loudly. New ale, wet wool and eels frying.
sites.source: Invented; an ale-house is the brief's word for it. Riddling at drink: the Exeter Book riddles (texts_793.json). After 886 an ale-house of the same kind stands inside the walls near the hithe (the game's assumption).

sites.name: The breaking beach
sites.see: The upstream end of the hard, where a big clinker ship lies on her side half stripped, her strakes coming off one by one and the iron clench bolts dropping into a basket. Beside her a new keel is set on blocks and a wright sights along it with one eye shut. Heaps of Roman tile and ragstone carted from the old city wait to make somebody a hearth. Tar smoke, adzes, oak chips underfoot.
sites.source: Clench bolts from a large clinker ship broken up on the foreshore, and 300 kg of Roman tile and ragstone, found behind the Strand (dossier 2 [N]). A yard is not recorded: this is where the game puts repair and building, before 886 here and after it on the shore below the walls (?).

sites.name: The pens by the north ditch
sites.see: Hurdle pens on trampled ground at the town's north-east edge, with a boundary ditch beyond and then open pasture and wood. Red cattle, a few sheep, pigs under an oak. A herdsman leans on a pen with two long-legged hounds lying at his feet, not for sale until the price is right. Butchers work at a bench by the ditch and the hides go on frames. Dung, blood and wet dog.
sites.source: Stock pens and a boundary ditch at the north-east (Parker House); butchers; hides as an export (dossier 1, 2, 4 [N]). Hounds as an English export are the spine's (thread counts_day) (?). Later values: an ox a mancus, a cow 20 pence, a pig 10, a sheep a shilling (the peace-guild's rules, about 930-939, dossier 7).

sites.name: The graves on the western rise
sites.see: A rise at the west edge of the town above the gravel pits, with graves among thorn trees. Two of them are stone coffins older than anybody's grandfather, carved by the Romans and used again. There is a standing cross of wood and, some say, a small church (?). A priest walks out from Saint Paul's for burials. Wind in the thorns, the river bright below, quarrymen shouting.
sites.source: Saint Martin-in-the-Fields: Roman sarcophagi, one of about 410, reused for Saxon graves with glass palm cups, perhaps the site of a church; no church is known inside the wic; gravel quarries to the west at the National Gallery, 2.75 m deep (dossier 2 [N, SM]). The cross is invented (?).

sites.name: Saint Paul's in the old city
sites.see: Twenty minutes' walk east, over the Fleet and in by a gate with no doors, among brambles and fallen walls two miles round. On the western hill stands the bishop's church with a few houses for his clergy about it; men with carts are pulling down a ruin nearby for its stone. Inside, candle wax and cold, and the shrine of Bishop Earconwald with a small wheeled chair kept beside it. Rooks in the broken towers.
sites.source: Saint Paul's, founded 604, its early form unknown; the walled city in ruins and robbed for rubble in 793 (dossier 2, 8 [N]). Earconwald, bishop 675-693, feast 30 April, lame with gout, went about in a small wheeled chair, and lies here (dossier 6, 7 [Er]). After 886 the town is all around it; Aelfheah is buried here 1012-1023 and Saint Edmund's body lodged in London 1010-1013 (dossier 6).

sites.name: Aethelred's hithe
sites.see: An inlet cut into the river bank below the old south wall, with a timber front and gravel hard, and ships lying stem-in before fenced plots that run back to a street. Each plot has its own posts: that is the bishop of Worcester's, that the archbishop's. An old stone building, roofless at one end, serves as a store. Porters, a clerk with tablets, the tide slapping under the planks, pitch and fish.
sites.source: S 346 (889): Hwaetmund's stone by the trading shore, trade on the public street or the shore paying the king. S 1628 (898 or 899): plots at Aethelred's hithe for Bishop Waerferth and Archbishop Plegmund with ship stations before the wall (dossier 2). Later Queenhithe.

sites.name: The toll at Billingsgate
sites.see: A gap in the river wall just below the bridge, with a hard and a row of posts. A tollman stands on a block with a boy beside him holding a bag; he looks at each hull and says a number before she has touched. A tall-sided hulk from the Rhine is unloading grey cloth and small kegs under his eye; men of Rouen roll wine casks and argue in Romance. Blubber, vinegar, pepper when a sack is opened.
sites.source: IV Aethelred 2, about 1000: chronicle_793.json 1000-london-tolls; Thornbury 1878 (dossier 4, 8: checked against the game's table and Thornbury only). No Billingsgate in 793 (dossier 8); the year the toll began there is not known, 990 is the game's (?).

sites.name: The bridge
sites.see: A timber bridge on many piers from the town to the south work, the river heaping against it on the ebb with a noise like a mill. Ships bound upstream lie below it waiting for slack water; small boats shoot the gaps and are sworn at. From the middle the whole town shows: the wall, the hithes, the bishop's church, smoke going up straight on a still morning.
sites.source: First mentioned when a widow who drove iron pins into a man's image was drowned at London Bridge, 963-975 (?) (dossier 7 [At]). Cnut's ships dragged round it in 1016; Godwin's fleet passing it by the south bank on the flood in 1052 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). No bridge in 793 (dossier 8). Olaf pulling it down in 1014 is saga only and is not used.

sites.name: The Danes' graves at Saint Paul's
sites.see: The south side of the bishop's churchyard, where the newer graves are. One has a slab set on edge, painted dark blue, red and white, with a great backward-looking beast on it tangled in a snake, and a line of runes cut along the rim. An old housecarl stands looking at it with his hat in his hand. Bells, lime trees, and from the street the cry of a man selling eels.
sites.source: The rune stone from Saint Paul's churchyard, laid by Ginna and Toki, of Cnut's time, with traces of its paint: Wikipedia (en) 'English Runic Inscription 2' (dossier 3, 6 [R2]). Saint Clement's as the Danes' church is tradition only (dossier 6).

sites.name: Saint Peter's on Thorney
sites.see: Upriver past the fields of the old wic, an island of thorn and gravel where two streams run into the Thames. A dozen monks keep a small church of Saint Peter and a landing with a fish weir. From about 1050 the east end is all scaffolding: masons from over the sea are raising a stone church longer than anything in the kingdom. A salmon is hung up in the porch once a year.
sites.source: Dunstan's monastery of about 959 with a dozen monks; King Edward's church, hallowed 28 December 1065; the fisherman said to have seen Saint Peter on Thorney, hence the abbey's yearly salmon: Wikipedia (en) 'Westminster Abbey' (dossier 2, 7 [WA]). Nothing of this in 793 (dossier 8).

people.name: Wighelm
people.trait: The king's wic-reeve on the Strand: witnesses every sale, enforces the ban on Frankish ships with regret and a private price.
people.want: The ports open again, and the first good cargo after the peace to pass through his hands.
people.fear: King Offa, who beheaded a king in 794; after 796, the men who remember whose reeve he was.
people.voice: Courteous, slow, asks the same question twice to see if the answer changes.
people.looks: About forty-five, grey-fair, clipped beard, a green cloak with a gilt disc brooch, a short sword, a rod of office, two armed men behind him.
knows: which ships he has turned away this month, and which he let land and why
what a sale needs to stand in law: witnesses, or himself
what the king has said about the Franks, and what the king has not said
who holds a ship free of toll here and by whose charter
what Abbot Gervold wrote last, if he trusts you

a shipmaster of his own port, sealed up on the Canche; the reeve's letters ask after him

Tilred at the Stour landing: he looks over the Kentish tallies for the king once a year and has never found the toll short, which worries him

lines.greet: Whose man are you, and from where? Dorestad. A Frisian, then, and not a Frank. And whose man did you say you were?
lines.greet_again: The same keel, the same master. I remember what you declared last time, and it was true. Come up to the hall when she is dry.
rumour: I turned a Frank away at the last spring tide. Good wine, too. The king's word is the king's word, and I am fond of my neck.
The king wants black stones cut to a length he remembers from his youth. If you know a quarryman on the Rhine, I know a king.
A sale without witnesses is a theft waiting for a name. Bring two honest men, or bring me. I am dearer, but I do not move away.
lines.saying: Ask a thing twice. The truth comes out the same both times; a lie has grown by the second.
lines.after_796: The old king is dead and I am still reeve. I would rather you did not remark on it where people can hear.
lines.to_heir: Your father stood where you stand and answered me the same way twice. That is rarer than silver here. Sit down.
lines.farewell: Take the ebb at its second hour and keep to the north side past the Fleet. And if anyone at Quentovic asks, I turned you away.

people.source: invented (the spine's cast.wighelm); the office is the wic-reeve of Lundenwic in the laws of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16. Offa had King Aethelberht of the East Angles beheaded in 794 (chronicle_793.json). No reeve is recorded turning Franks away (dossier 8). His kin at Sarre is this file's invention (?).

people.name: Ibba
people.trait: One of King Offa's moneyers, who puts his own name on every penny he strikes and so can never deny one.
people.want: Good silver in and good pennies out, and no man clipping between the two.
people.fear: A light penny with his name on it laid in front of the king.
people.voice: Short, exact, talks while he weighs and does not look up until the pan is still.
people.looks: About forty, thick forearms, a leather apron scorched at the lap, hair tied back, a touchstone on a thong at his neck and black under every fingernail.
knows: what the new heavy penny weighs against the old light one, and what he gives for a Frankish denier
which foreign silver is good: he has cut most of it
the names of the other moneyers on the king's coin, and which of them he would trust
that Eoba, who struck pennies in the queen's name, works at Canterbury and not here (?)
how much silver went through the port last moon, which is how much trade there was

ties.note: each thinks the other takes too much from a stranger
has never met the Dorestad moneyer and knows his coin by its feel; says it is honest and dull
English pennies go into Gerwin's pot and come out Frankish; Frankish ones do the same here. They have never met, and know each other's work by the weight
Lul strikes for the East Angles' king and then for Offa; a moneyer changes his die, not his trade
the comb-maker cuts his balance pans' bone pointers and is paid in new pennies, not old
Thiadbod once brought him a bag of bad deniers and smiled; Ibba is waiting to return it
Eoba signs for the same king at Canterbury, and for the queen: each says the other's pennies are a grain light

lines.greet: Deniers. Put them in the pan. You get the king's pennies for the weight, less my cut, less the fire. Sigh at the fire, not at me.
lines.greet_again: You again. Your silver was good last time. That is the only thing I remember about anybody.
rumour: The king made the penny heavier and broader. The old light ones go in the pot. Bring them before the reeve sees them, not after.
They say King Charles has made his own penny heavier too. Two kings who will not speak, agreeing about silver. Silver is the better envoy.
A Dane paid a weaver in a cut ring last month. She brought it to me in tears. It was better silver than the king's.
lines.saying: My name is on the penny. The king's face is only on the front.
lines.to_heir: Your father never brought me a bad coin. Once he brought me a strange one, with writing like worm tracks. I kept it.
lines.farewell: Count them before you leave the bench. After the door, they are yours.
lines.gold: Look, do not touch. The king's name in the middle, and round it marks no priest can read. I cut them as I found them. Tell me if you ever see their like.

people.source: Ibba is a moneyer named on Offa's pennies, very probably of London: Naismith, British Numismatic Journal 80 (2010) (dossier 3 [Na]). Nothing else is known of him: his age, years, manner and ties are invented (?). Eoba struck at Canterbury (dossier 8). The heavy penny of 792/3: dossier 4. The coin 'like worm tracks' is a dirham (thread silver_road).

people.name: Tatberht
people.trait: An Englishman who lodges Frisians, answers for them in law and has picked up their tongue, their thrift and their jokes about Franks.
people.want: To keep the yard in his family's hands, and every bed in the loft paid for by Martinmas.
people.fear: Fire in the thatch; and a guest of three nights who does a thing the host must answer for.
people.voice: Easy and unhurried, half English and half Frisian in one sentence; counts guests on his fingers while he talks.
people.looks: About forty-five, broad and stooped from low doorways, brown beard going grey, a russet tunic, a ring of keys and a knife at his belt, a sheep's bone he whittles at when idle.
knows: which Frisian ships are on the beach, whose they are and when they mean to float off
what the law makes a host answer for, to the day
what wine and querns fetched on the hard this week, because his guests complain to him
where a boy of a foreign house could be left to learn English and the trade
the family tale that a Frisian of this yard once bought a thegn no fetter would hold (?)

ties.note: his younger sister; she sends him drunk guests and he sends her thirsty ones
names his guests to the reeve, as a host must
his grandson, who has the yard after him
Thiadbod takes the best bed and pays on the day, every time; Tatberht does not like him and cannot say why
the pilot sleeps in his loft between tides and pays in news of the sands
remembers him as a boy learning the Thames marks from Gerlef
hosts on both shores send their guests on to each other with a token
the widow's cloth is stored here by the season; she has never been cheated and says so
the priest buries the guests who die in his loft and writes to their kin; he pays for the wax
the host on the strand at Eoforwic: they pass each other guests and warnings, and each has fewer Frisians than his father had

lines.greet: Dorestad? Then you sleep here. One night you are a guest, three nights you are my trouble. Leave your knife on the peg.
lines.greet_again: Your bed is where it was. Nobody has died in it since. Sit, eat, and tell me who is on the water.
rumour: A Frank's ship lay off the hard two tides and was not let land. He sold his wine to a Frisian over the side. Everybody saw; nobody witnessed.
The wic was busier in my father's day. Now the plot next door is a midden. A midden pays no dues, I will say that for it.
A Frisian of this yard once bought a captive no chain would hold. Let him go for a promise, and was paid. We still tell guests.
lines.saying: A guest is like fish: the third day you know.
lines.after_fire: It burned from the bakers' end with the wind behind it. I got the guests out and the keys. The keys fit nothing now.
lines.to_heir: You have your father's way of looking at the roof before you sit. He paid for part of that roof. Your bed is free.
lines.farewell: Float off on the flood and God keep you off the sands. If you see my sister, I never said anything about her ale.

people.source: invented. The name is one scratched in runes on a sheep's backbone from London (?) (dossier 3). The host's liability after three nights: Hlothhere and Eadric c. 15 (npc_text_encounters.md 1.1; wording to check). The captive is Imma, 'sold at London to a Freson' in 679 (Bede IV.22); that the buyer's house was this yard is a family boast and the game's invention (?). The saying turns a proverb of guests and fish that is older than its first English record (?).

people.name: Leofrun
people.trait: Keeps two looms and four girls, makes the cloaks the Franks buy, and has an opinion on kings who measure them.
people.want: An order large enough to set up a third loom, paid half beforehand.
people.fear: A bad year for wool; her eyes; a letter between two kings that fixes the length of her work.
people.voice: Brisk and dry, talks with her hands full; ends an argument by going back to the loom.
people.looks: About thirty-three, lean, strong hands, hair under a linen cap, a grey gown pinned at the shoulders with two plain bronze pins, a bone weaving sword stuck in her belt.
knows: what a cloak costs in wool, days and dye, and so what it must sell for
the old length and the new: she can cut either and says which wastes less
which Frisian pays on the nail and which pays in promises
when the wool comes in and from whose flocks it is worth having
what the Frankish buyers ask for, since they ask her first

ties.note: her elder brother; she keeps his tallies because he cannot
every bale she sells to a stranger goes past his rod
the widow buys her cloaks by the score and has never tried to beat her down twice
the count's steward at Dorestad has an order with her for one cloak of the old length, unpaid
her cousin Hildgyth under the wall at Dofras; they ask each other in every message why the Franks want them longer
buys his fleece on the tally and pays when the cloaks sell
West Saxon cloth goes out through Hamwic while her port is shut, at her price

lines.greet: Looking or buying? Looking is free until you touch. That one is sold. That one is sold. That one you cannot afford.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who paid. Come in, mind the weights. I have six finished and two on the loom, and I know what you gave last time.
rumour: They say the Frankish king complains our cloaks are short. He buys them by the piece and wants them by the ell. So would I.
A short cloak is the same work at the loom and less wool. Whoever started cutting them short was no fool, and was not me.
Wool was dear after the wet spring. If your king wants the old length he can have it at the old length's price.
lines.saying: Measure the buyer first, then the cloth.
lines.to_heir: Your mother's cloak was mine, I would know that selvedge anywhere. Tell me it wore well. Lie if you have to.
lines.farewell: Keep them dry and folded, not rolled. And if a Frank asks who wove them, say a woman who expects to be paid.

people.source: invented. Looms in almost every house of the wic and cloaks as its export: dossier 1, 4 [N]. The cloaks 'at the old length': Charles to Offa, 796 (dossier 4 [Of]). The emperor's complaint about short cloaks sold at the old price is Notker's story of the Frisians' cloaks (Gesta Karoli I.34, tr. Grant 1907), not quoted here.

people.name: Hunfrith
people.trait: A comb-maker who can price a stag's antler at a glance and cannot keep a tally to save his life.
people.want: Good antler in quantity, and a buyer who takes combs by the hundred instead of by the one.
people.fear: His sister reading his tallies; the cough that comes of bone dust.
people.voice: Cheerful, vague about numbers, exact about teeth to the inch; coughs between sentences.
people.looks: Nearly forty, thin, white dust in his hair and beard, a fine-toothed saw in his hand, a leather apron, three finished combs stuck in his belt like knives.
knows: which antler is worth carrying: shed or cut, red deer or the big northern kind he has only heard of
who in the town works horn, bone, leather and wire, and whose work is honest
what combs fetch across the water, from Frisians who told him too much
where the old pit is that his master filled with spoiled blanks
that Northmen sell hones at the beach some summers and say very little

ties.note: his sister; he fears her more than the reeve
cuts bone pointers for the moneyer's balances
three notches on the stick over her door are his
the Gipeswic potter's crates come up the river packed in straw and, when he remembers, antler (?)
a comb-maker at Hamwic who cuts runes on his work; Hunfrith says a comb does not need to be read
a Dane who sold him hones and one great antler, and asked more about the river than a hone-seller needs

lines.greet: Combs? A man who buys one comb has lice. A man who buys a hundred has a ship. Which are you?
lines.greet_again: I owe you, or you owe me. My sister will know. Sit there, not there, that is the saw.
rumour: A Northman showed me an antler as long as my arm, flat like a hand. He said the beasts pull sledges. I said nothing; he was large.
My old master dug a pit for his spoiled combs. Seventy, I counted once. A man is known by his pit.
The wire-drawer next door has a new die. Now every brooch in the town has the same face. Go and look.
lines.saying: Every tooth is cut one at a time, and the comb is sold all at once. That is the trade.
lines.to_heir: Your father brought me antler when nobody else would carry it. Bone dust and all. Here, this one is not for selling.
lines.farewell: If you see antler anywhere north of the Humber, think of me before you think of the price.

people.source: invented. The Bedford Street pit with the waste of 65 to 70 combs, about 730-750; a jewellery workshop; Norwegian hones (dossier 2, 4 [N]). The 'flat' antler is reindeer (goods_793.json antler; Ohthere's tame deer, texts_793.json ohthere). His tie to the spine's Asulf is this file's invention (?).

people.name: Eanwulf
people.trait: A priest of the bishop's church who walks out to the wic to bury its dead and hear its oaths, and misses the books he was taught from.
people.want: One good book for a church that has few: he will pay to have it brought, and pay more to have it copied.
people.fear: Fire among ruins, where nobody keeps a bucket; dying somewhere there is nothing to read.
people.voice: Gentle, bookish, falls into a list when nervous; names the saint of the day before he says good morning.
people.looks: About forty, tall, tonsured, ink on two fingers, a dark worn cloak over a white tunic, a small book in a leather satchel he never sets down.
knows: which feast is next and whose fast is today
who the bishop is this year and whether he is at home: Coenwealh, then Eadbald, then Heathoberht, who dies in 801
how a buyer swears at the altar that he bought openly in the wic
the tales of Bishop Earconwald: the wheeled chair, and how the Londoners carried off his body from the monks of Chertsey
what the archbishop fears in Kent, when the archbishop is this side of the Medway

ties.note: carries the archbishop's letters between Saint Paul's and the Kentish shore; in 796-798 Aethelheard is out of Kent
heard Alcuin teach at York for one winter and has lived on it since (?)
Alcuin's letter-carrier lodges with the clergy when he passes
the reeve sends men to him to swear; he sends the reeve men who have sworn falsely
buries the yard's dead guests and writes to their kin
the same archbishop, at his own landing
Eadhun of Christ Church: each has been trying to borrow a book off the other for ten years

lines.greet: God be with you. It is Saint Alban's eve, did you know? No. Well. You have come from over the water; have you any books aboard?
lines.greet_again: The merchant who listens. Good. I have a letter for the Kentish shore and nobody honest to carry it. You see where this is going.
rumour: The heathen have burnt Saint Cuthbert's church in the north. I have read the letter. I read it twice and then I went and counted our buckets.
The king wished the archbishop's seat moved here to London. Rome said no. I would have had neighbours who could read.
Our old bishop Earconwald went about in a little chair on wheels. We keep it by his shrine. The sick touch it; the children want to ride it.
lines.saying: A book is the only cargo that is worth more after it has been used.
lines.to_heir: Your father carried a book up this hill wrapped in his own cloak, in rain. I say his name at Mass. You may carry the next.
lines.farewell: Go with God. Mind the Fleet at the flood, it is wider than it looks. And if you see parchment for sale anywhere, remember me.

people.source: invented; no priest of 793 is named (dossier 8). The bishops and their years: dossier 3 [B]. Earconwald's chair and the carrying off of his body: dossier 7 [Er]. The oath 'at the altar': Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16 (dossier 6 [HE]). Leo III's refusal of 798: dossier 5. Aethelheard out of Kent 796-798: the spine. Saint Alban's feast is 22 June. That he heard Alcuin at York is invented (?).

people.name: Wynflaed
people.trait: Brews for four peoples, keeps the peace among them with a ladle, and forgets no debt and no face.
people.want: Every crew that drinks here to pay before it floats off; failing that, to know where it lives.
people.fear: A fight with knives in it, for which the house answers; sour ale in a hot week.
people.voice: Loud, quick, kind underneath; answers a riddle before the asker has finished and is usually right.
people.looks: About thirty-five, sturdy, red forearms, a striped apron over a brown gown, a string of glass beads, an iron ladle she points with.
knows: everything said in her house in the last month, in any of four tongues
which crews are short a man, and which men are short a crew
who owes whom on the beach: the stick over her door is only the start of it
more riddles than a monk, and the rude answers to the clean ones
when the reeve is in a mood to turn ships away, from how his men drink

ties.note: her elder brother; she thinks he is soft on Frisians
he owes her, three notches deep; she lets it stand because he makes her laugh
his crew drank a winter's ale and floated off on the dawn tide; he says he knew nothing of it
an English hand who once kept a knife fight out of her house by sitting on a man
the old pilot drinks one cup, slowly, and tells her the sands
pilgrims say the ale is better at Dover; she says pilgrims will say anything
the ale-wife at Hamwic tells the onion riddle too, and each says she had it first (?)
the ale-wife in the old baths at Legacaestir: word and barm go between them with the lead carts

lines.greet: A new face. Sit where I can see your hands. Ale is a farthing's worth of your silver the cup; news is free if you bring some.
lines.greet_again: You. You paid last time, I looked at the stick. Your corner is free, and the eel is fresh if you are quick.
rumour: The reeve's men drank quiet last night. When they drink quiet, somebody is being turned away at the next tide. Is your master a Frank?
A crew in from the north coast would not say what they saw. Then they drank, and said. Go and ask the priest about buckets.
There is a hand in the corner whose ship left without him. He rows, he does not steal, and he owes me. Hire him and pay me.
lines.saying: A man is thirstiest just after the mead. That is the whole of my trade.
lines.riddle: I stand up in a bed, hairy underneath, and make a churl's daughter weep. Say what I am. No, the other answer. Onion.
lines.to_heir: I knew your father's notches, and he always cleared them. You start with a clean stick. Do not make me cut it.
lines.farewell: Pay, then go. If you drown, I am telling everyone you owed me.

people.source: invented. The riddle is the Exeter Book's onion (texts_793.json exeter_25_onion; Tupper 1910), paraphrased, not quoted. The saying turns one of the Durham Proverbs, 'sometimes men are thirstiest after the mead' (our rendering (?)). Her price is said loosely: there was no farthing coin, a cup is paid in cut pennies or on the stick (?).

people.name: Ceolmund
people.trait: Tatberht's grandson, who keeps the yard through the slaughter of 842 and the storm of 851 and gives the plot its name.
people.want: A ditch, a fence and a boat tied where he can reach it; and one quiet year.
people.fear: Sails in the lower river on a spring tide at dawn.
people.voice: Flat and watchful; breaks off in the middle of a sentence to listen to the river.
people.looks: About forty, spare, a burn scar down one forearm, a patched russet tunic like his grandfather's, a ring of keys, a spear leaning inside the door, a sheep's bone with runes on a thong.
knows: what was on the beach the morning after, in 842, and who got out
where the ditches are and which roads they cut
who is buying plots cheap, and it is bishops
what the king takes now for weighing and measuring in the port
which Frisians still come, and that they come under a Dane's leave

ties.note: his grandfather; he has the bone and the keys
after 850 his Frisian guests sail by Rorik's leave, and he has learned to ask to see it
a Dorestad skipper who still makes the crossing and still takes the same bed
sends the ealdorman of Kent word of sails in the Thames and is sent word of the Wantsum back (?)

lines.greet: Frisian? Show me whose leave you sail by. Good. The loft is dry. If I say run, leave the cargo.
lines.greet_again: Still alive, both of us. That is twice. Sit with your back to the wall, it is the custom here now.
rumour: They came on the flood at first light. By the ebb there was nothing on the beach that could carry a man. I still count hulls each morning.
The bishop of Worcester is asking after plots by the west gate. A bishop buys when honest men sell. Draw your own conclusion.
The king's man weighs everything now and the king is paid for the weighing. The penny is half copper. I weigh it too.
lines.saying: My grandfather feared fire. I would be glad of only fire.
lines.to_heir: This bone was my grandfather's. He kept a bed for your house, and so do I, while there is a roof over it.
lines.farewell: Go down on the first of the ebb, not the last. And look behind you at the Nore.

people.source: invented. The name is taken from the plot 'Ceolmundingchaga' (Ceolmund's enclosure) granted to Bishop Alhhun in 857 (S 208, dossier 2); who the real Ceolmund was is not known, and this man is the game's guess at him (?). The slaughter of 842 and the 350 ships of 851: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Ninth-century ditches at Maiden Lane and Long Acre (dossier 2 [N]). Hamwic laid waste in 842: Nithard IV.3 (realms/england_south.md). Rorik at Dorestad from 850: the spine.

people.name: Brihtwold
people.trait: The king's tollman at Billingsgate, who can tell a keel from a hulk at three hundred paces and says the rule aloud to every one.
people.want: The right toll from every hull, and the Emperor's pepper weighed in his own pan, not theirs.
people.fear: Ninety-four sails; and being the man who let the wrong ship lie inside the bridge.
people.voice: A crier's voice, flat and carrying; says every rule as if for the first time today.
people.looks: About forty-five, bald, weathered, a blue cloak with a silver ring pin, a tally board on a strap, a boy beside him with a bag and a horn.
knows: the toll by the ship: a halfpenny, a penny, fourpence, and what the men of Rouen pay on wine and blubber-fish
what the Emperor's men give at Christmas and Easter, to the glove
who has the king's leave to lie inside the bridge
what the town paid the army last time and what it is asked for now
that no man buys goods over twenty pence outside a port, and what happens when he does

ties.note: stood on the wall in 1009; after 1012 has to count the same man's ships as the king's
from 1016 the toll is Cnut's, and he reads it out in the same words
not the man, long dead, but his heirs' merchants: the men of Rouen are his oldest customers and worst arguers
the Gipeswic moneyer sends word of fleets with his complaints about the dies; Ipswich was harried in 991 and 1010
the reeve of Hamtun feeds the same fleet he counts; they compare sums
the Wantsum sees every sail a day before he does, and Leofnoth sends a rider
the king's earl at York, to whom he writes when a fleet is spoken of in the river (?)
the moneyer strikes what he collects; they have counted the same tribute from both ends

lines.greet: Small boat, a halfpenny. Sail, a penny. Keel or hulk, four, if she lies here. You are a keel. Do not tell me you are a boat.
lines.greet_again: The same keel, the same fourpence. I knew her by the patch in the sail before I knew you.
rumour: The Emperor's men brought the pepper at Easter, ten pounds, short by a spoon. They said it dried on the Rhine. Pepper is dry already.
The men of Rouen say their duke shelters our king. Then they argue the toll on his own river. Wine and blubber, six shillings, I did not make it.
The town has paid before and is asked again. Everybody on this bank knows his share to the penny, and the name of the man who shirked his.
lines.saying: The tide takes nothing from you that it did not bring. I am not the tide.
lines.to_heir: I took your father's fourpence for twenty years and he never once told me she was a boat. You may lie to starboard, by the post.
lines.farewell: Clear the hard before the next one touches. And tell them at home what the toll is, so I need not.

people.source: invented; the office and the rule are IV Aethelred 2, about 1000 (chronicle_793.json 1000-london-tolls; dossier 4; the six shillings on a large ship of Rouen's is from the chronicle entry's note (?)). No buying over 20 pence outside a port: II Aethelstan 12 (Thatcher 1907). Ninety-four ships in 994; Ipswich harried 991 and 1010: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

people.name: Cynred
people.trait: A Mercian dealer in fleece and hides who sells on the tally to half the weavers and shipmasters of the south, and sleeps badly.
people.want: To be paid, in the king's new pennies, by men who are at present on the wrong side of a closed sea.
people.fear: A debtor's ship sealed in a Frankish port with his wool in her; a wet shearing.
people.voice: Mild and patient, with a long memory for sums; says 'when it suits you' and means Martinmas.
people.looks: About forty, round-faced, a sheepskin jerkin over a good blue tunic, a bundle of notched tally sticks tied with a thong at his belt, lanolin-soft hands.
knows: what fleece and hides cost at the pens this week, and what they will cost after the shearing
which flocks up the Thames valley have the long wool the cloak-makers want
who owes him: a wool man at Hamwic for half a thin year's fleece, and a shipmaster whose cargo is spoiling on the Canche
what the Frankish fairs paid for English wool before the ports were shut
which herdsman has hounds worth a count's silver

ties.note: sold him Mercian fleece on credit in a thin year and has been paid half; they are still friends, which is how he means to get the rest
the wool in the sealed ship on the Canche is his until it is sold; he counts the days too
Leofrun buys on the tally and has never been late; he gives her first pick
every bale that goes to a stranger is witnessed, and he pays for the witnessing
the Frisian offers a tenth of its worth for wool that is in trouble, smiling

lines.greet: Wool or hides? Feel that. That is from above Dorchester, the long kind. I can let you have it on the tally if the reeve knows you.
lines.greet_again: You paid on the day. I cut the stick in two and burned my half. Sit; there is new fleece in from the valley.
rumour: I have wool in a ship on the Canche with a Frankish seal on her hatch. Every wet day I feel it in my teeth.
A wool man at Hamwic owes me for half a year. He says his port is open. I say then he can afford to pay.
The herdsman by the ditch has two hounds a count would hang a man for. He will not sell them apart, and he is right.
lines.saying: Wool on the sheep is the shepherd's, wool on the tally is mine, wool on the sea is God's.
lines.to_heir: Your father took my wool over when nobody would carry it, and brought the silver back counted. I have a bale put by for you.
lines.farewell: If you touch at the Canche, ask after a sealed ship. And tell her master I am not angry. Yet.

people.source: invented, to stand where the writers of Hamwic and Quentovic put a wool man of Lundenwic (hamwic.leofstan, quentovic.leofstan). Wool as a likely export, hides and the stock pens: dossier 2, 4 [N]. Selling on a split tally is the general practice of the time; none survives from the wic (?).

people.name: Wynsige
people.trait: Ealdorman Aethelred's reeve at the hithe in the new town inside the walls: shares out the shore in plots, takes the king's part of every sale, and holds the hostages of men who trade across the line.
people.want: Every plot at the hithe let, every ship at her own station, and no Dane in the town he cannot name.
people.fear: The army back in the Lea or at Benfleet; a hostage's kin who do not come back.
people.voice: Brisk and legal; says 'by the ealdorman's leave' the way other men say 'God willing'.
people.looks: About forty, lean, close-cropped, a grey cloak with a silver strap-end at the belt, a wax tablet in one hand and a measuring cord with knots in the other, a clerk behind him.
knows: which plots at the hithe are the bishop of Worcester's and the archbishop's, and what a ship station costs
the rule of the peace with Guthrum's people: no crossing without leave, trade only with hostages given
what pays the king on the street and the shore, and that the bishop weighs in his own court
who came in from the north with walrus teeth and a story for the king
what the men of London did at Benfleet and on the Lea

ties.note: holds the Dane's surety from the year he first crossed the line to trade, and has come to like him
King Alfred's daughter, countess over the water: his lord's wife's sister, whose merchants land at his hithe
passed the Northman and his teeth up to the king, and was thanked
another seafarer with a tale for the king; he has learned to send such men upriver
the ealdorman who bought the gold-lettered gospels back from the army: in his last years he still sends to the hithe to ask which of the army's men are selling (?)

lines.greet: By the ealdorman's leave you may lie here one tide. After that you lie at a plot-holder's station or you pay for mine. Whose is it to be?
lines.greet_again: The same master. Your station is free, and nothing was said against you while you were away. That is not true of everyone.
rumour: The bishop of Worcester has the old stone house by the shore now, and weighs in his own court. On the open street the weighing is still the king's.
A Northman came in with teeth as long as my forearm and rope cut from one hide. I sent him to the king. One does.
We took their ships on the Lea, the ones worth taking. The rest we broke up. There is good oak cheap on the shore this month.
lines.saying: A wall is only stone until somebody inside it pays his share.
lines.to_heir: Your father's name is on my tablet among those who gave a surety and came back for it. Not all did.
lines.farewell: Out on the ebb, and show your leave at the Lea mouth if you are stopped. They are mine there.

people.source: invented, to stand where the writers of Ganda and Gipeswic and the walrus_ivory chain put a reeve of Alfred's London (the chain says the forge names him: this row gives the name). Alfred and Aethelred, 886; S 346 and S 1628 (dossier 2, 4); Benfleet 893 and the ships on the Lea 896 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 894, 896); the treaty of Alfred and Guthrum on hostages and trade (the spine, thread price_of_england). Aelfthryth, Alfred's daughter, married Count Baldwin II of Flanders; Aethelred's wife was her sister Aethelflaed.

people.name: Thorkell
people.trait: A sea-king for hire: takes East Kent's three thousand pounds, tries to buy the archbishop's life from his own drunken men, then sells his ships to the English king.
people.want: Pay, and a lord worth serving.
people.fear: His own army at a feast.
people.looks: Very tall, in his forties, a long moustache, a mail shirt and a gilded helmet, a great axe, forty-five ships at anchor behind him in the Thames.
knows: what the army has been paid and what it expects
which of his shipmasters will buy wine, cloth and mail, and pay in English pennies by the bag
what happened at Greenwich on the Saturday after Easter in 1012, and he does not tell it the same way twice
where the fleet will lie this winter
after 1017, what the king thinks of earls who are taller than he is

ties.note: the same person
after 1016; outlawed 1021, reconciled 1023
his greatest earl and the one he trusts least
the tollman remembers him on the wrong side of the wall
his army landed at Sandwich in 1009 and East Kent paid three thousand pounds; the reeve who carried Sarre's part has kept the tally sticks
the moneyer whose pennies paid him to go away and then paid him to stay; he thinks well of a man who does both jobs cleanly
a herring-master of Dommoc whose sister's house his army burned: as earl he takes a share of the catch and is given it, exactly weighed
a shipman of Rouen who buys from his quartermasters and sold his army wine at Sandwich
the moneyer whose town he burned in 1010: as earl he dines there, pays for what he drinks, and takes the third penny of the mint
the reeve of Hamtun, on whose beach his quartermasters bought with other men's pennies; the reeve counted every one
a Dofras house that paid into the three thousand pounds of 1009 and tells the sum over every winter
the archbishop at Rouen buys back, at a price, church plate his men sold on the Seine strand, and says what he thinks of the sellers
the bishop at Ripa has said aloud what he thinks of a chief who was paid to change sides and paid again to stay
a farmer of the Svear who pulled an oar in the fleet and went home with English silver and a by-name; one of several thousand, and paid like the rest (?)

lines.greet: A merchant! Good. My men have silver and nothing to spend it on but each other. What have you got that is not ale?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the honest scales. Sit. Drink. Then tell me what mail fetches in your country, and do not be modest.
rumour: We tried this town more than once and it stood. I do not mind saying so. A wall that stands is worth being inside of.
I offered them gold and silver for the old bishop, everything but my ship. They were drunk on southern wine. I will not speak of it again.
Forty-five ships took the English king's pay with me. Ask the others why they did not. Some of them cannot answer now.
lines.saying: Serve a lord who pays. If none pays, be one.
lines.to_heir: Your father sold me wine when nobody else would come alongside. I pay my debts. Some of them in silver.
lines.farewell: Go, then. If anyone stops you in the river, say my name. If it does not help, say it louder.

people.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1009-1023; Thietmar of Merseburg VII.42-43 for his offer to ransom Archbishop Aelfheah, 'all but his ship' (?); chronicle_793.json 1009-08-thorkell, 1012-04-19-aelfheah (the spine's cast.thorkell). His faith and his birth year are not recorded (?). His words are invented.

people.name: Cnut
people.trait: A conqueror who becomes a careful Christian king: pays off his fleet, keeps forty ships, gives to churches, and bargains with emperors over merchants' tolls.
people.want: One peace on both shores of the North Sea, and his merchants free of unjust tolls on the road to Rome.
people.fear: What happens to it all when he dies.
people.voice: Formal, through writs and reeves; a merchant hears him as a law read out.
people.looks: About thirty, tall, fair, a long nose (so later writers say (?)), a crown and a gold-hilted sword on feast days, housecarls with gilded axes behind him.
knows: what the town owes him, to the pound, and that it has paid
which merchants hold his writ and what it frees them of
what he asked of the Emperor and the king of Burgundy at Rome in 1027 about tolls on the road
where his forty ships lie and who pays their crews
which saint he means to honour next, and with whose silver

ties.note: the same person
his greatest earl, outlawed in 1021 and reconciled in 1023
made him earl, then outlaw, then earl
kept the old tollman and the old toll: a new king who changes nothing at the waterside is forgiven a great deal
the moneyers of the old king strike the new king's face from 1017, and are left at their benches
the earl of the Northumbrians came to submit in 1016 and was cut down in the hall with forty men, by Thurbrand, and by the king's leave (?)
the king at Dyflin strikes pennies after his pattern and sends ships in his peace (?)
kept the old king's moneyers at their benches and only changed the face on the die
the reeve who stood at the gate of Hamtun when the great men rode in to swear, and was left in his office
the reeve on the Wantsum who once paid his father's allies to go away, and was told to move an island out of a saint's road
made him an earl and gave him a Danish wife; everything the house of Godwine has began with that
a boy of Dofras at the oar in one of the ships called out for the king: the fleet was his school
the bishop at Ripa sends him word of Jutland by merchants bound for London
the archbishop at Rouen is his queen Emma's brother
a shipman of Rouen with wine and barrelled whale: the men of Rouen keep their old terms at the London hithes under him, and pay one king where they paid three
the richest man in York, who bowed with the north in 1016 and kept his house and his silver by it (?)
the men of Tiel lie at his hithes in every season: he has never heard this one named, and has made the road to Rome cheaper for all such men (?)
one of the Svear paid off from the fleet with the great tribute of 1018: the king knows the sum, not the man (?)

lines.greet: The king greets all his people in friendship. You are a merchant from over the sea. You will have his peace while you keep his law.
lines.greet_again: The king knows your name. It was read to him among those who paid what was due and asked for nothing.
rumour: The fleet has been paid and sent home. Forty ships remain. The king wishes it known that forty is enough.
The king has spoken with the Emperor at Rome. Merchants and pilgrims of his lands are to go and come without unjust toll.
The holy archbishop is to be carried home to Canterbury. The king's guard will keep the bridge while it is done. Do not be on the bridge.
lines.saying: A king's peace is like a sail: it serves on both tacks or it is no use.
lines.to_heir: Your house served the king's father's enemies and then the king. It is not held against you. It is remembered.
lines.farewell: Go in the king's peace. Show the writ when it is asked for, and not before.

people.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1014-1035; Cnut's letter of 1027 on the tolls; chronicle_793.json 1016-10-18-assandun, 1018-heregeld, 1027-03-26-cnut-rome, 1035-11-12-cnut-dies (the spine's cast.cnut). A merchant meets him through a reeve reading his words, which is why the lines speak of him as 'the king'. The carrying of Aelfheah to Canterbury in 1023 with the guard keeping the Londoners away: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1023; Osbern, later. The words are invented.

people.name: Æthelstan
people.trait: The first king of all the English: a gatherer of relics, books and other kings' sons, who rules by councils and has it written down what a port is for.
people.want: One coinage in every port, every large sale made before a reeve, and thieves ridden down by the men they robbed.
people.fear: The north, which has sworn to him and is waiting; and what follows a king with no son of his own.
people.voice: A merchant hears him as a law read out by the bishop and the reeves: numbered, careful, sure of being obeyed.
people.looks: About thirty-five, slight, of middle height, fair hair bound with gold thread (so a later writer says (?)), a crowned head on his pennies, a gospel book carried before him by a clerk.
knows: what may be bought outside a port and what may not: nothing over twenty pence
how many moneyers each port is allowed: eight at London, two at Hamtun, seven at Canterbury
what the bishops and reeves of London have sworn among themselves about stolen stock
which foreign princes eat at his table, and which of them he means to send home with ships

ties.note: his godson and foster-son, the Breton count's heir bred at his court: in 936 he gives him ships to go home in (?)
his father's sister, the old countess in Flanders, whose merchants land at the hithe and ask after Wessex bread

lines.greet: The king greets his bishops and his reeves in London. No man is to buy goods above twenty pence outside a port. You are in a port. Buy.
lines.greet_again: The king's law has not changed since you were last on this hithe. That is what a law is for.
rumour: There are to be eight moneyers in London and one coinage in all the king's land. A moneyer found false loses the hand he struck with.
The bishops and reeves of this town have sworn to ride after stolen cattle together, and to pay a man for what he lost. A thief over twelve winters is not spared.
A Breton lord's son has grown up at the king's table. The king is giving him ships. Somebody on this hithe is going to be asked for a pilot.
lines.saying: A port is a place where a sale has witnesses. Everywhere else it is only two men and a horse.
lines.farewell: Go in the king's peace. Sell before the reeve, and you will have no need of an oath afterwards.

people.source: Æthelstan, king 924/5 to 27 October 939 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). Ports, witnessed buying and moneyers: II Æthelstan 12-14, about 928 (chronicle_793.json; dossier lundenwic 4); the ordinance of the bishops and reeves of London: VI Æthelstan (dossier lundenwic 6, 7; not quoted, Attenborough 1922 is not free). Alan of Brittany as his foster-son, sent home in 936: the Chronicle of Nantes, a later text (?); places/namnetis.json ties its Alan to this id. Ælfthryth of Flanders was his father's sister. A merchant meets him through a reeve reading his words. His looks are William of Malmesbury's, two centuries on (?); the words are invented.

people.name: Eadwold
people.trait: A moneyer of London in the tribute years: has struck one king's face to pay another king's army, and then the second king's face with the same hammer.
people.want: Good dies cut cleanly, old pennies brought in when the type changes, and nobody leaving for Denmark with a debt at his bench.
people.fear: A light penny with his name on it found in a Dane's bag; fire in the lane.
people.voice: Quick, dry, a townsman's: counts while he talks and never loses the count.
people.looks: About forty, narrow shoulders and thick wrists, a clean leather apron, a short grey beard, a bunch of iron dies in a box he keeps a foot on.
knows: what the town paid in 1018, to the pound, and how many blows of the hammer that was
when the type changes and what he gives for the old pennies
which Danes and Svear went home rich, and which went home owing
that the dies for the ports down the coast are cut here, and what their moneyers say of the cutting

ties.note: the Gipeswic moneyer gets his dies from this lane and complains of them by every keel; Eadwold keeps the complaints in a bowl
a Svea who went home with English silver and a debt at this bench, and means every year to send it (?)
the tollman gathers what he strikes; they have counted the same tribute from both ends
struck the old king's face, then the new king's, with the same hand
struck the pennies that paid the tall Dane to go away, and then the ones that paid him to stay

lines.greet: Old pennies or foreign silver? Either way it goes in the pot and comes out the king's. Sit down. It is not quick and it is not free.
lines.greet_again: Your silver was good last time. I remember silver. Faces I leave to the tollman.
rumour: Ten thousand five hundred pounds from this town alone. I struck my part of it. My arm knew the sum before the reeve read it out.
A Svea left for home owing me for forty pennies' change. He said he would send it. That was before the king went to Rome.
The dies for Gipeswic go down by keel. Their man says my cutter cannot spell his town. His town cannot spell itself.
lines.saying: A king's face wears off a penny in ten years. The moneyer's name is on the other side, where the thumb does not rub.
lines.farewell: Count them here. And if you sail for the Svear, there is a man called Sigvid. Tell him I can still count.

people.source: Eadwold is a moneyer's name on London pennies of Æthelred II and Cnut, from memory of the Swedish finds' lists (Hildebrand 1881), not rechecked (?); a moneyer of the same name signs at Canterbury about 997-1003 (dossier fordwic 3), who may or may not be the same man (?). Everything else is invented. He stands where places/uppsalir.json (Sigvid's debt 'at a moneyer's bench' in London) and places/gipeswic.json (the dies cut in London) need a moneyer of this age: the bench of 793 is Ibba's (lundenwic.moneyer). London's 10,500 pounds: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1018.

people.name: Wulfgar
people.trait: King Edward's port-reeve in London: greeted by name in the king's writ beside the bishop, and answerable for every keel from Rouen, Flanders and the Emperor's land that touches the bank.
people.want: The king's customs whole, the burgesses quiet, and the men of Rouen made to pay what the men of Flanders pay.
people.fear: Earl Godwine's ships below the bridge and the king's French friends above it, on the same tide.
people.voice: Even and official; names the king first in every sentence and himself not at all.
people.looks: About forty-five, grey-fair, a trimmed moustache, a dark blue cloak with a silver brooch, a white rod, a clerk with a writ in a leather case.
knows: what a keel pays at Billingsgate and what the men of Rouen say they paid last time
whom the king's writs greet in the town: the bishop, the port-reeve and all the burgesses
which reeves down the coast take more than the customs allow
where the earl's ships lie, and whose side the shipmen of the town are on this month

ties.note: the port-reeve at Canterbury's landing: they compare what the men of Rouen paid at each bank, and it is never the same
the earl has the shipmen's love and a third penny in half the ports of the south; the reeve has only the king's writ

lines.greet: The king greets his bishop and his port-reeve and all the burgesses of London. I am the port-reeve. You are a keel, and owe fourpence.
lines.greet_again: The same house, the same fourpence. The king's customs do not grow because a man is known. Nor shrink.
rumour: The men of Rouen say the reeve at Fordwic took more from them than I do. I have written to ask him. He has written back very warmly about the weather.
The king is building a great church upriver on Thorney, in the Norman manner. The stone comes by sea. Somebody is being paid well for the carrying.
When the earl's ships came up to the bridge the shipmen of this town did not hurry to stop them. I say no more than was seen.
lines.saying: A writ is a short thing. Everything it leaves out is the reeve's work.
lines.farewell: Clear the bank before the next keel. Greet the reeve at the Stour from me, and count your change there.

people.source: Wulfgar the port-reeve is greeted with Bishop Ælfweard in a writ of King Edward for London, 1042 x 1044 (Sawyer 1103; dossier lundenwic 3). Nothing else is known of him: his years here (the game keeps him to 1052 (?)), his looks and his words are invented. After him the dossier names Ulf the port-reeve and Esgar the staller. He stands where places/fordwic.json needs a reeve of London for Bruman to compare customs with.

stories.title: Whose man are you?
stories.summary: While the two kings will not speak, the wic-reeve turns Frankish hulls off the hard and asks every Frisian the same question twice. He would rather the ports were open, he writes to the abbot who keeps the Frankish tolls, and he needs somebody neither English nor quite Frankish to carry it.
stories.picture: A reeve in a green cloak on a gravel beach at low water, rod in hand, two spearmen behind him, looking up at a Frisian skipper on a beached ship; a Frankish hull riding off in the stream behind, not let land.

beats.text: Quernstones finished for the English trade stand unsold on the dam, and skippers argue whether a king's order binds Frisians. Somebody has to go and find out.
Wighelm comes down the beach before the keel is dry. A Frank he turns away. A Frisian may land for a gift and a story, or wait a tide on his pleasure, or go round by Hamwic.

beats.when: year < 797 and flag.bs_ban_heard and not flag.bs_peace
beats.text: In the hall he asks for a quiet ship. There is a letter for the abbot's clerk at Quentovic, and a rod cut to the length of the stones his king remembers.
Hildric breaks the seal behind the toll table. An English ship lies roped on the bank with her wool going sour, and a favour may be asked instead of silver.
At Saint-Wandrille a monk says what the quarrel was about: not stones or cloaks, but a daughter asked for and a daughter asked back.
The answer and a knotted cord come back to the reeve. Leofrun wants to know why Franks want cloaks longer. Thiadbod, whose ship always lands, would pay for the answer to go astray.
The reeve has King Charles's letter read out on the hard: the ports are open, merchants have protection, true pilgrims pass free. The first Frankish wine in years is sold by dark.

The wic-reeve comes down the strait in his green cloak to look over his sister's husband's tallies. Dunwalh has counted the abbess's ships again. Wighelm asks him the number twice, and then asks a Frisian on the strand whose man he is.
Since the East Angles' king lost his head the reeve's word runs to the Orwell. Eadstan reads it out slowly beside a Mercian clerk, and the tallies he sends back to the Strand come late.
A notched tally from the Strand, saying this Frisian has been looked at, is honoured by the young Mercian who watches the bishop's haven. He asks his three questions all the same.

endings.how: You carried the letters both ways, kept the seals whole and were on the hard when the peace was read.
endings.text: The first good cargo after the peace passes through Wighelm's hands, and it is yours. He witnesses it himself and takes no fee.
endings.reward: The chain's silver (800 to 1500 d by the ending) and a standing order for quernstones; unlock_charter_lundenwic; the reeve a fast friend (lundenwic.unlock.reeves_witness).

endings.how: You would not pay the reeve's private price and took the road round by the West Saxon wic.
endings.text: Your stones reached England by the back door and sold dear. Wighelm heard, and is polite about it. He asks you everything three times now.
endings.reward: A high price for quernstones while the ban holds; the way to unlock_factor_hamwic or unlock_pilot_solent in the chain; the reeve cool.

endings.how: You let Thiadbod buy the abbot's answer, or read it yourself.
endings.text: The ports stay shut a season longer and one Frisian house grows fat on it. It is not yours, though you were paid. Leofrun's cloaks sit on the chest.
endings.reward: Silver now (900 to 1300 d in the chain) and a year of dear quernstones here; the abbot remembers (flag ch_black_stones_abbot_remembers); Wighelm wary for years.

stories.reward: A reeve who knows your word is the same the second time he asks: toll eased, sales witnessed at once, and the first place on the hard when the ports open.

stories.title: A cloak of the old length
stories.summary: The count at Dorestad will take an errand in place of part of his silver: English hounds for his hunting and a cloak cut as cloaks used to be. The hounds are at the pens and not for sale until the price is right; the cloak is Leofrun's to weave, and she wants half beforehand and a fortnight.
stories.picture: A weaver holding a long brown cloak up against a Frisian merchant to measure it, two lean hounds on a rope sniffing at the hem, looms and hanging clay weights behind.

beats.text: Hartwin lays the tally on the table and names the errand: two English hounds and a cloak of the old length, by Michaelmas, against a part of the debt.
Leofrun can cut the old length. It takes more wool and the same days at the loom. Half now, the rest when it comes off; or buy a short one today and hope the count does not stand up in it.
The herdsman's hounds are a bitch and a young dog out of the same litter. He will not part them and he will not be hurried. The reeve must witness, or the count's steward will ask whose they were.
A fortnight is a long time to feed a crew. Tatberht will keep the hounds in the cart shed; Thiadbod, in the best bed, offers to carry the whole errand home for you, as a kindness.
Hartwin shakes out the cloak and measures it against the count's own. The hounds are walked up and down. The tally is cut, or it is not.

Hildgyth under the wall at Dofras is Leofrun's cousin and still cuts the old length for those who ask. A cloak off her loom would pass at the count's table. Whether it would pass Leofrun, who hears of everything sold in Kent, is another matter.

endings.how: You paid Leofrun half beforehand, waited the fortnight, had the hounds witnessed and brought all three home sound.
endings.text: The count wears the cloak at his court and hunts with the hounds before the frost. Hartwin cuts the tally without comment, which from him is praise.
endings.reward: Part of the debt struck off (the thread's db_service cleared); Leofrun's third loom, and her cloaks at the maker's price ever after (lundenwic.unlock.leofruns_order).

endings.how: You bought a short cloak off the chest to save the fortnight.
endings.text: The count stands up in it. Hartwin says the king himself has an opinion about such cloaks. The hounds are accepted; the cloak is sent back with you.
endings.reward: Half the service counted; one short cloak to sell; Leofrun amused and no worse disposed.

endings.how: You let Thiadbod carry the errand home in his bigger ship.
endings.text: The count has his hounds and his cloak a week early, from Thiadbod's hand, with Thiadbod's compliments. Your part in it is not mentioned.
endings.reward: No days lost and no service cleared; Thiadbod's standing with the count rises (the road toward flag db_bought); Tatberht tells you what he thinks, once.

stories.reward: Debt worked off instead of paid, and a weaver at Lundenwic who sells to your house first.

stories.title: The name on the penny
stories.summary: King Offa's moneyers sign their coin, and from 793 the penny is heavier and broader than the Frankish deniers a Frisian carries. Ibba changes them at a loss and remembers every man's silver. Over the years the same bench strikes a gold piece that names the wic, and for one year a West Saxon's pennies.
stories.picture: A moneyer in a scorched apron at a counter, a small balance held up between finger and thumb with a foreign coin in one pan, a merchant watching the pointer; behind, a man swinging a hammer over a die block.

beats.text: Ibba weighs your deniers against the new heavy penny and gives fewer than you hoped. The old light English pennies are worse still: the reeve refuses them and the pot takes them.

Ibba takes a gold piece out of a rag: the king's name in the middle of a ring of marks no priest can read, copied from a coin a pilgrim brought home. He asks every man who has been east of the Elbe whether he has seen such writing.
Sigimar takes old deniers by weight less his cut. A bag of the old coin bought cheap here is only worth carrying to a bench that still wants silver more than it fears the king.
