At the Channel mint English pennies go into the pot and come out Frankish. Gerwin asks what Ibba gave you, and tells you what Ibba should have given.
A coin 'with writing like worm tracks' lies in the moneyer's pan of curiosities: good silver from beyond the Baltic. The bench will melt as many as you can bring, and asks where they come from.

King Coenwulf has gold struck: a piece worth thirty pennies with the words 'from the wic of London' on it. They are for giving, not spending. One is offered you for a service, or for thirty-five in silver.
The dies are new and the name on them is Ecgberht's, the West Saxon. The moneyer is the same man. He says a die is a die, and looks at the door.
Eoba at Canterbury asks what Ibba gave for a denier, weighs the answer, and says Ibba's letters are better than his sums. He has heard of the gold piece and would not copy a coin he could not read.
Lul on the Orwell changes at a loss like the rest and has heard of the gold piece too. A moneyer who has put a she-wolf on a penny does not laugh at another man's strange coin.

endings.how: You brought the bench good silver on three calls and never a bad coin.
endings.text: The moneyer stops cutting your coins and starts counting them. His cut is the king's and no more, and he tells you which pennies to refuse elsewhere.
endings.reward: lundenwic.unlock.moneyers_pan: coin changed here at half the loss; a true word on the weight of the penny, good for two years.

endings.how: You bought up light pennies and old deniers where they were refused and carried them to a bench that took them by weight.
endings.text: It pays once, handsomely. The second time the reeve is waiting at the bench with his rod, and your name is said aloud with the word 'light' beside it.
endings.reward: A quick profit (about a fifth on the bag); the thread's flag sv_old_coin if caught; Ibba cool, Wighelm wary.

endings.how: You did the bench or the king's reeve a service in Coenwulf's years and took the gold piece instead of silver.
endings.text: A gold penny with the wic's name on it rides in the chest of your house. Nobody will change it and everybody wants to hold it. Your heirs show it to moneyers.
endings.reward: An heirloom worth thirty pennies in silver and more in standing: shown at any English mint it opens the moneyer's talk (feeling toward the house raised).

stories.reward: A moneyer who knows your silver: less lost at every change, and warning before a coin goes bad.

stories.title: The yard by the west road
stories.summary: One fenced plot and the family that keeps it, across sixty years: a bed for Frisians, two fires, a slaughter on the beach, and at last a bishop's charter with the family's name on a plot it no longer holds. What the merchant's house does for the yard decides whether anybody in the town knows it afterwards.
stories.picture: A fenced yard at dusk seen from its gate: a long thatched house with a loft door open, a cask-lined well, a man whittling a sheep's bone on the step; beyond the fence a broken Roman wall and a church on a hill.

beats.text: Tatberht gives you a bed and the law: one night a guest, three nights his trouble. He scratches his name on a sheep's backbone in runes while he talks, and asks who is on the water.

A Frisian guest of the yard dies in the loft, on his third night. Tatberht answers for him and must bury him; the priest walks out from Saint Paul's, and somebody has to carry the dead man's chest and the word of it home to Dorestad.
A boy of your house may be left here to learn English and the trade. He is found some years later on the hard, beating an eel-wife down in her own tongue.
The town has burned and the yard with it: the house is posts and ash, the well is sound. Tatberht has the keys and nothing they fit. Thatch and timber for the row would cost three hundred pennies.
The widow Thiadburg asks after the yard where her cloth is stored, and whether there is a roof on it. She will put in a third if somebody she trusts puts in the rest.

You round the bend to a beach of burnt booths and no hulls. Ceolmund stands in the shallows with nine people and a sheep's bone on a thong. They offer everything for a passage out; you have room for six.
The bishop of Worcester is asking after the plot by the west gate, with its measure and weights. The king will grant it for sixty shillings unless somebody the family knows pays its dues first.
Inside the walls a host by the hithe has a sheep's backbone hung over his door and does not know what the scratches say. If your house does, the bed is free.

endings.how: You paid toward the roof after a fire and took the family off the beach in 842, all of them or the six you had room for.
endings.text: The family outlives the wic. When the town moves inside the walls a house by the hithe keeps a bed for yours, and tells its children why.
endings.reward: lundenwic.unlock.yards_bed for every heir: free lodging, a free corner of store, and the port's news told straight (it carries over the move of 886).

endings.how: You bought the plot when it was ash and cheap, and kept the family on it as your tenants.
endings.text: The yard is yours and the fence is mended. Ceolmund's name stays on it in every mouth but yours. In 857 the bishop's men go and ask about another plot.
endings.reward: unlock_plot_lundenwic at half price (250 d) from 798; a store of your own; the family loyal while the dues are fair. A raid year takes the stock unless it was moved.

endings.how: You slept there for years and gave nothing when it burned or when the fleet came.
endings.text: By 857 the plot is the bishop of Worcester's, with its measure and weights, and a stranger has the key. He charges a penny a night and has never heard of your house.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but what was never bought: lodging at the common price, and no line 'to_heir' from anyone on this shore.

stories.reward: Somebody on the Thames who knows your house for three generations.

stories.title: What the town paid
stories.summary: London is bought and sold four times in a hundred and fifty years: an army winters in it and is paid to go, a king takes it and walls it, a fleet fails against it and is paid anyway, and a Dane is crowned and sends it the bill. A merchant can pay a share, sell to the men who were paid, or do both and be remembered for each.
stories.picture: Silver pennies being poured from sacks onto a cloth spread on a river hard, a tollman with a tally board counting, the timber bridge and a line of dragon-prowed ships at anchor behind under a low sky.

beats.text: The army has its winter quarters here. It buys ale, meat and cloth with other people's silver and sells what it carried off. Upriver a bishop is selling land to pay his share, in the year the pagans sat in London.
The great army has crossed from England and winters on the Scheldt, selling English plate and English people. Some of what lies on the bank was last seen on the Strand.
King Alfred has the town, and Ealdorman Aethelred keeps it. The trade is moving inside the old walls; plots at the hithe go to bishops, each with a ship station in front.

The dies for the tribute's pennies are cut in London and sent down the coast by keel. Leofsige at Gipeswic strikes his town's share with them and complains of the cutting to every master who will listen.
Brihtwold reads the toll to every keel. Beside you the Emperor's men hand over pepper, gloves and vinegar. Everybody on the bank knows his share of the last tribute, and the next.

Beaten off from London on the Nativity of Saint Mary, the ninety-four ships lie the winter at Hamtun. The reeve there feeds the fleet that the tollman at Billingsgate counted from the wall, and they compare sums by letter.
Thorkell's army lies at Sandwich and East Kent has paid three thousand pounds. His shipmasters have pennies by the bag and nothing to buy. Whoever sells to them is asked about it at Billingsgate.
East Kent's three thousand pounds are gathered at every landing from the Stour to the strait. What each keel paid there is known at Billingsgate within the week, by name.
The archbishop the army killed at Greenwich lies in Saint Paul's, and the town that would not fall prays at his grave. The tall Dane who tried to buy his life now takes the English king's pay.
Ten thousand five hundred pounds from London alone. Then the fleet is paid off, forty ships stay, and the king's writ keeps a merchant from Ribe to the Thames. The town's part is still being counted.
English pennies are everywhere on the Schlei, and men home from England have more than they can spend. A Londoner would know some of the coins by the moneyer's name.

endings.how: You were asked for a part of the town's tribute and paid it without being made to.
endings.text: Your name is on the tollman's good side of the board, with the citizens. Under Cnut the men who paid are the men who are heard.
endings.reward: The thread's flag en_paid_share; the toll here at a citizen's rate; the way to the king's writ (flag en_cnut_peace: lundenwic.unlock.kings_writ).

endings.how: You sold wine, cloth or mail to the fleet that had just been paid.
endings.text: It is the best market of your life, by the bag and unweighed. At Billingsgate afterwards the tollman says the rule to you a little louder than to the others.
endings.reward: The thread's flag en_followed_silver: a great profit once; Thorkell and his shipmasters friendly; Brihtwold cool, and the town remembers it for a generation.

endings.how: You paid your share and also sold to the fleet, and told no lie about either when asked.
endings.text: Nobody likes it and nobody can fault it. The Danes call you the Frisian with the honest scales. The English call you the same, in a different voice.
endings.reward: Both flags; trade with both sides at a small discount in feeling; under Cnut, who was both sides, it stops mattering and the writ is yours for the asking.

stories.reward: A standing in the walled town that outlasts three conquests: the toll at a citizen's rate and a king's writ.

stories.title: Water made bone
stories.summary: At Fordwic a riddle answered to the reeve's face passes a ship free of toll, and the king's wic-reeve at Lundenwic will not be outdone by a Kentish landing. He has a riddle of his own, two lines long, about a thing every shipman has cursed in a hard winter; he gives it to masters whose answers he has learned to trust, and the same freedom goes with it.
stories.picture: The king's hall in the wic on a winter morning: a reeve in a green cloak laying a wax tablet face up on a table of tally sticks, frost on the rushes by the open door, a Frisian master frowning at the tablet with his cap in his hand.

beats.text: Tilred passes a ship free for Tatwine's sword answered to his face. Word of it goes up the Thames with the next keel, and the wic-reeve asks every Kentish master whether it is true, and then asks again.
Wighelm pushes his tally sticks aside and says a thing he has by heart: a wonder on the wave, water become bone. He says it twice, as he says everything, and waits to hear whether the answer changes.
Wynflaed has the answer before the asker has finished and will not sell it. The reeve, she says, can tell a bought answer by the way it is carried up the hill.

Eadhun sells Tatwine's leaf of snow, hail and ice for twelve pennies, and says the old archbishop needed snow, hail and ice together for what the reeve's English does with ice alone. He wants the English written down.
The riddle has outlived the wic. A reeve at the hithe inside the walls asks it of masters he likes, in the same words, and does not know which of the men before him began it.

endings.how: Took the riddle away, worked it out on a cold passage, and gave the answer to the reeve's face.
endings.text: Wighelm asks for it once more, to be sure. Then he cuts no notch for your keel, and says the Kentish reeve may keep his sword: his own riddle is shorter and his beach is longer.
endings.reward: rw_toll_lundenwic (riddles_793.json): no toll on your ship at Lundenwic for some years (the card sets unlock_charter_lundenwic for four years); the deed won_riddle; Wighelm friendly.

endings.how: Carried the reeve's two lines to Christ Church and let the scribe write them down beside Tatwine's.
endings.text: Eadhun writes the English under the Latin and looks at the two for some time. He says the archbishop would have liked it, and sells you the Latin leaf at a friend's price.
endings.reward: Tatwine's leaf of snow, hail and ice (the text tatwine_15_nive_glacie) at half its price; Eadhun friendly; a riddle that is now in a book.

endings.how: Said the first thing that came, at the table, in front of the clerk.
endings.text: The reeve does not say it is wrong. He asks whose man you are, as he did the first day, and the riddle goes back under the tally sticks until the next hard frost.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but a try and a little pride; the riddle rests, and wakes when ice is seen or spoken of.

stories.reward: A ship free of toll at Lundenwic for some years, and a reeve who asks you a third question for pleasure.

works.name: A fenced plot in the wic
works.what: An enclosure with a house, a store and a cart shed, held of the king for a yearly due, with the right to use measure and weights there 'as is the custom in the port'.
works.needs: To be well regarded at the port and known to the reeve, who witnesses the bargain (unlock_plot_lundenwic). After the fires of 798 and 801 a burnt plot goes for half.
works.gives: A stock of your own here: buy cloaks and wool in the cheap season, sell wine in the dear; a free berth and roof for the crew; a factor needs it. A raid or burning takes the stock unless it was moved.
works.picture: A plot fenced with wattle hurdles on a gravel road, a long thatched house end-on, a barred store, a balance hanging in the doorway, a reeve driving in a boundary stake.
works.source: S 208 (857): the plot Ceolmundingchaga with measure and weights as is the custom in the port (dossier 2); story/unlocks_793.json unlock_plot_lundenwic (its price and yearly due). Plots as rubbish dumps by 793 (dossier 1 [N]).

works.name: A length of timber front on the hard
works.what: Oak piles and planks a metre high along your own width of the shore, with two mooring posts and the ground behind raised and gravelled so a cart can come to the ship's side.
works.needs: A plot here, the reeve's leave, and oak: the timber is felled in winter and the work done between spring tides.
works.gives: Your ship loads and unloads in half the time and needs fewer porters; she can lie at your own posts through a neap. It is known as your front, which is a kind of standing.
works.picture: Men standing in river mud driving an oak pile with a great maul, a row of planks already pegged behind it, a cart tipping gravel, a beached ship waiting alongside.
works.source: The stake-and-wattle and oak pile-and-plank fronts with mooring posts, and ground raised to +1.6-2.0 m with gravel yards, at York Buildings and the Adelphi (dossier 2 [N]). No quay or jetty: it is a revetted beach (dossier 8).

works.name: A cask-lined well
works.what: A well dug through the gravel in a yard and lined with two old Rhenish wine casks set one on the other, their heads knocked out.
works.needs: A yard to dig it in (your own plot, or Tatberht's with his leave) and two sound casks, which a wine carrier has anyway.
works.gives: Clean water for a crew and a house; one fewer way for a fire to win. The neighbours draw from it and remember whose it is.
works.picture: A man waist-deep in a round pit lowering a big silver-fir cask into it on ropes, a second cask waiting, a woman with a yoke and two buckets looking on.
works.source: Barrel-lined wells in the wic and a silver-fir wine-cask head from the Strand (dossier 2 [N]).

works.name: Thatch and timber for the burnt row
works.what: After the fire, posts, wattle, daub and thatch to put a roof back on Tatberht's yard and the two houses beside it before winter.
works.needs: One of the fires (798, or 801) to have happened; silver in hand. The widow Thiadburg at Dorestad will put in a third if asked.
works.gives: The yard stands and its people are yours for good: free lodging, the row's weavers selling to you first, and a name in the town for coming back when it was ash (the story lundenwic.the_yard).
works.picture: A burnt street of black posts under a grey sky with one house newly framed in pale timber, men passing bundles of reed thatch up a ladder, a host with a ring of keys watching.
works.source: The fires of 798 and 801 (Historia Regum, a twelfth-century text (?); dossier 5, 8); a burnt sill-beam house at the Adelphi (dossier 2 [N]). The yard and the widow's third are invented.

works.name: A ship station at Aethelred's hithe
works.what: A share of the piling and the hard before a plot inside the walls, with the right to moor along its own width and trade there, leased from a bishop who holds the plot.
works.needs: A plot in the town (unlock_plot_lundenwic) or a lease from the bishop of Worcester's or the archbishop's man; year 889 or later.
works.gives: A mooring that is yours by right inside the walls: no waiting for a place, goods carried straight to your own store, and trade on your own ground (story/unlocks_793.json unlock_work_lundenwic_hithe).
works.picture: A timber river front under an old stone wall, mooring posts with a ship stem-in between them, a fenced plot running back to a street, a clerk in a cowl pointing out where the boundary runs.
works.source: S 346 (889) and S 1628 (898 or 899): the plots of Bishop Waerferth and Archbishop Plegmund with ship stations before the wall (dossier 2); story/unlocks_793.json unlock_work_lundenwic_hithe.

works.name: A gift to the restoring of Saint Paul's
works.what: Silver toward timber, lead and a mason's wages after the bishop's church burned, given at the altar and written down by the clergy.
works.needs: The fire of 961 to have happened. Nothing else: the bishop takes any Christian's silver.
works.gives: Your house's name is said at Mass in the bishop's church; the clergy lodge your letters and vouch for you; the townsmen's feeling toward you rises. A grave in the churchyard may be asked for.
works.picture: A church with a charred roofless nave and new pale rafters going up, a merchant laying a bag on the altar step, a priest writing in a book propped on his knee.
works.source: Saint Paul's burned and was restored the same year: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 962 as printed (dossier 5). Names of givers read at Mass is the general custom of the time; a list at Saint Paul's is not recorded (?).

ships.how: bought second-hand on the breaking beach, or built to order over a winter
ships.note: The ship that crosses from the Rhine mouth: about fourteen metres, five men, six tons, a flat keel so she sits upright on the hard. Old ones end their days here and are broken up for their iron; a sound one can be had from a skipper who is giving up the sea.
ships.picture: A broad clinker cargo ship with one mast lying dry and upright on a gravel beach at low water, a plank from her side to the shore, a second one half broken up beside her.
ships.source: Clench bolts from a large clinker ship broken up on the Strand foreshore (dossier 2 [N]); the Graveney boat, about 895 (Design/content/ships.md); story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_north_sea_merchant_ship (Lundenwic is named).

ships.how: lent by a bishop or a minster, never owned
ships.note: The bishop of Rochester has had one ship free of the king's toll at London since 733, and the minster in Thanet another. Such a ship needs a master the church trusts; while you sail her the toll is not taken on her.
ships.picture: A plain sturdy coaster on the hard with a small wooden cross lashed at her stem, a cleric handing a rolled charter to her master, the reeve standing by with his rod lowered.
ships.source: S 88 (733, confirmed 844 x 851), S 86 and S 143 (dossier 4); story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_coaster_minster_ship and unlock_charter_lundenwic.

ships.note: Every house on the shore keeps one for the eyots, the Fleet and the far bank, where there is no bridge. About 1000 the toll at Billingsgate asks a halfpenny of such a boat.
ships.picture: A short flat plank boat with one pair of oars drawn up on cobbles beside a much larger hull, an eel basket in her bottom.
ships.source: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_skiff_punt (Lundenwic is named; forty pennies); IV Aethelred 2 (dossier 4).

ships.how: not bought: a place at the steering oar of a levy ship, as a duty
ships.note: Alfred's long ships of 896 were crewed in part by Frisians, and three are named among the dead. In 1008 the king orders a ship from every 310 hides. A shipowner trusted in the town is told to bring his men and steer, or pay for one who will.
ships.picture: A long low rowing ship with thirty oars a side lying in the river below a walled town, a steersman at the side rudder, shields along the rail.
ships.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 896 (897 as printed), 1008; story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_warship_west (Lundenwic is named; the game allows it from 800, this file from Alfred's ships). The 'naval men' of London in the 1030s (dossier 3).

sayings.text: A mart of many peoples coming to it by land and sea.
sayings.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History II.3, of London (our rendering); dossier 1

sayings.text: The reeve wants to witness every sale. A man cannot sell an egg in this town without a king's man watching.
sayings.source: story/sayings_793.json say.inv.c.reeve (invented in the period's manner; Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16)

sayings.text: Buy in the wic and bring the reeve; buy in the dark and bring a priest.
sayings.source: invented, turning Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16: a buyer without witnesses must swear at the altar that he bought openly in the wic

sayings.text: Sold on the flood, regretted on the ebb.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: ships are run onto the hard at high water and sit dry at low (dossier 1)

sayings.text: The king measures the cloak; the weaver measures the king.
sayings.source: invented, from the cloaks 'at the old length' in Charles's letter to Offa of 796 (dossier 4)

sayings.text: Sometimes men are thirstiest after the mead.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs (an eleventh-century collection; our rendering (?))

sayings.text: Oft they fought against the city of London; but glory be to God, that it yet standeth firm.
sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1009 (Ingram 1823 (?), as the dossier gives it); said in the town from 1009

sayings.text: He died as he stood at his drink. There are worse ways, and the feast went on to the end of the cask.
sayings.source: invented, on King Harthacnut's death at Lambeth, 8 June 1042 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1042, our rendering); said from 1042
invented: a tollman's answer to the Emperor's men when the Easter pepper is short (IV Aethelred 2); said from about 1000

sayings.text: A Frank is turned away, a Frisian is asked twice, and a Dane is not asked.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, for the years of the ban (about 789 to 796); no reeve is recorded turning Franks away (dossier 8)

easter_eggs.text: The host whittles at a sheep's backbone and has scratched his own name on it in runes: Tatberht. Ask, and he shows you which stave is which.
easter_eggs.source: A name in runes on a sheep's backbone from London (?) (dossier 3)

easter_eggs.text: Clench bolts by the basketful on the breaking beach, each one bent where it was drawn: a big ship is being unmade plank by plank. A boy will sell you a handful for a farthing's worth of bread.
easter_eggs.source: Clench bolts from a large clinker ship broken up on the Strand foreshore (dossier 2 [N])

easter_eggs.text: The well in the yard is lined with a wine cask of a pale soft wood that does not grow in England. Its head, with a bung hole, serves the dog as a dish.
easter_eggs.source: A silver-fir wine-cask head from the Strand: the wood is of the upper Rhine (dossier 2, 4 [N])

easter_eggs.text: Two of the graves on the western rise are stone coffins cut by the Romans. In one of them, beside a Saxon's bones, lies a small glass cup with no foot, made to be held in the palm until it is empty.
easter_eggs.source: Roman sarcophagi reused for Saxon graves with glass palm cups at Saint Martin-in-the-Fields (dossier 2 [N, SM])

easter_eggs.text: By the shrine at Saint Paul's stands a small chair on wheels. Bishop Earconwald, lame with gout, went about his diocese in it; when he died at Barking the Londoners carried off his body from the monks of Chertsey.
easter_eggs.source: Wikipedia (en) 'Earconwald', after Bede IV.6 and the later Life (dossier 7 [Er])

easter_eggs.text: About 805 to 810 a gold piece is struck here with the words DE VICO LVNDONIAE, 'from the wic of London'. One was dropped by a river forty miles north and lay there until 2001. It sold for 357,832 pounds.
easter_eggs.source: The Coenwulf mancus found at Biggleswade: Wikipedia (en) 'Coenwulf of Mercia' (dossier 4, 7 [Co])

easter_eggs.text: A Frankish monk on the beach has a parchment by which King Offa gave his abbey of Saint-Denis land 'in the port called Lundenuuic'. The reeve reads it twice, as he does everything, and says the king's clerk does not make his letters like that.
easter_eggs.source: S 133, a charter of Offa dated 790 for Saint-Denis, forged at the abbey (dossier 7); the scene is invented, and the forgery may be later than this (?)

easter_eggs.text: Boniface stood on this beach in 716, paid his fare to a shipmaster and sailed for Dorestad. An old woman in the ale-house says her grandmother sold him bread and he blessed the loaf and not her.
easter_eggs.source: Willibald, Life of Boniface c. 4 (dossier 4 [Wb]); the old woman is invented

easter_eggs.text: A fisherman on Thorney says Saint Peter himself once hailed him for a crossing and paid him in salmon. The monks hang one up in the porch every year, and take a tenth of the catch.
easter_eggs.source: Wikipedia (en) 'Westminster Abbey': the legend of the fisherman and the yearly salmon (dossier 7 [WA])

easter_eggs.text: The slab on the Danes' grave reads, in runes along its edge, that Ginna and Toki had this stone laid. It does not say for whom. The beast on its face looks back over its own shoulder.

In 1051 the goldsmith Spearhafoc, bishop-elect of London and never consecrated, is gone overnight with the gold and gems he was given to make the king a crown. A skipper at the hithe remembers a heavy chest and a passenger who did not want his name asked.
Bridge folk tell of a widow who drove iron pins into a man's likeness. She was drowned at the bridge, and that is the first time anybody wrote the bridge down.
easter_eggs.source: A charter of 963-975 (?) on the forfeiture of an estate (dossier 7 [At]); not quoted

easter_eggs.text: In 1040 fishermen draw up a king in their net: Harold, called Harefoot, dug up and thrown into the fen by his brother's order. The Danes of the town bury him decently in their own graveyard.
easter_eggs.source: Wikipedia (en) 'Harold Harefoot', after John of Worcester (dossier 7 [HH])

easter_eggs.text: Ibba keeps a gold piece in a rag: OFFA REX in the middle of a ring of marks nobody in England can read. They were copied stroke for stroke from a coin a pilgrim brought home, and they are the Saracens' writing, their caliph's year and the profession of their faith, with the king's name set in upside down to them. One such piece will be bought in Rome a thousand years on.
easter_eggs.source: Offa's gold dinar in the British Museum, copied from a dinar of the caliph al-Mansur dated AH 157 (773-774) and said to have been got in Rome (?); the spine's easter egg for thread silver_road ('a moneyer shows a gold piece with marks nobody can read, copied from a coin a pilgrim brought'). That the moneyer was Ibba is the game's

unlocks.what: A ship free of the reeve's toll at Lundenwic
unlocks.how: Master a bishop's or a minster's ship (unlock_ship_coaster_minster_ship), or win the reeve's leave by carrying the letters of the black stones chain to the peace.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_charter_lundenwic: 'show the charter' at the hall or the toll does toll none on that one ship while she carries the church's goods with yours.

unlocks.what: A fenced plot of your own in the port
unlocks.how: Before 871: bought from the reeve by a house well regarded here, for 500 d (250 d for a burnt plot after 798, in the story lundenwic.the_yard). From 889: leased from a bishop at the hithe.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_plot_lundenwic: a stock of your own, a winter berth, a roof for the crew; the house works are built on it.

unlocks.what: A man of your house at Lundenwic
unlocks.how: Hold a plot here or be a friend of a host (Tatberht or his heirs); then 120 d. Also the fruit of leaving a boy on the Strand in the chain house_heir.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_factor_lundenwic: a factor who keeps stock, buys cloaks and wool in the cheap season and sends prices home by any ship.

unlocks.what: The Thames sands and the tide to the Strand by heart
unlocks.how: Hire the pilot on three calls and come up without touching; or sail it three times yourself; or be taught it over a winter by Gerlef, who sleeps in Tatberht's loft.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_pilot_thames: no pilot's fee, the sands passed as sure, and the flood taken at the right hour instead of a six-hour wait.

unlocks.how: From 889, with a plot in the town: pay your share of the piling and the hard (the work lundenwic.work.ship_station).
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_work_lundenwic_hithe: your own ship station inside the walls and trade on your own ground.

unlocks.what: The reeve witnesses your sales himself, at once and for nothing
unlocks.how: Answer Wighelm the same way on three calls with nothing hidden, or carry his letter and bring back the answer with the seal whole.
unlocks.gives: Every sale here stands in law without a wait or a fee (act:witness free and sure); the toll eased by a third while he is reeve; half of it passes to his successor for your heir.

unlocks.what: The moneyer counts your coin instead of cutting it
unlocks.how: Bring the bench good silver on three calls and never a bad coin (the story lundenwic.name_on_the_penny).
unlocks.gives: act:change_coin here at half the loss; a true word on the penny's weight and on which coins to refuse, which is news worth carrying to Dorestad and Quentovic.

unlocks.how: Pay Leofrun half beforehand once and take delivery when she says, or bring the count his cloak of the old length (the story lundenwic.old_length).
unlocks.gives: act:buy_at_source at her looms a fifth under the street's price, and a standing commission: she weaves six for your next call.

unlocks.what: Credit and first news at the ale-house
unlocks.how: Clear your crew's notches every time for a year, or pay off the hand she vouches for and hire him.
unlocks.gives: act:drink and act:rumours on the stick when silver is short; rumours here are a week fresher for you than for a stranger; she warns you when the reeve means to turn ships away.

unlocks.what: A bed for your house on the Thames, for every heir
unlocks.how: Pay toward the roof after a fire (lundenwic.work.row) and take the family off the beach in 842 (the story lundenwic.the_yard).
unlocks.gives: Free lodging and a free corner of store here in every generation, before and after the town moves inside the walls; the host's line 'to_heir' and the port's news told straight.

unlocks.what: A brother of the Londoners' peace-guild
unlocks.how: From about 930: hold a plot in the town, be vouched for by two brothers, and pay fourpence a year.
unlocks.gives: Goods stolen from your store or ship here are ridden after by the brothers and paid for at the guild's values (an ox a mancus, a cow 20 pence, a horse half a pound); a thief knows it, so theft cards here go against him.

unlocks.how: From 1018: have paid a share of the town's tribute without being made to, or be vouched for by Thorkell while he is in favour; then an audience and a gift.
unlocks.gives: The thread's flag en_cnut_peace: the king's peace on your ship from Ribe to the Thames while he lives, and the toll here at a citizen's rate. It ends with him in 1035.
